subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext:
But there is no doubt in my mind that Dr. Morgentaler would not be in jail if he had not done something that can be called courageous. I agree he broke the law. That has been confirmed. Also, I abide by the decisions of our courts. But there is an element of courage in what he did. Today, 116 doctors in the province of Quebec admit that they, too, commit illegal abortions and that they conspire in these acts. I suspect that the number
May 29, 1975

is closer to 800, not 116. The whole hypocritical sham that has developed around this subject needs correction.
One of the reasons we come to the House to debate the subject, no matter which side of the argument we support, is to get to the question of finally resolving the issue. One of the ways is to establish more therapeutic abortion committees, but another way-and it seems to me the only one that ultimately will be satisfactory-is to remove the subject from the Criminal Code and allow a person to follow the dictates of his or her conscience on this subject. This is not a matter of abortion on demand-that is a ridiculous claim-it is a matter of the conscience of the individual in possession of professional advice. I see no reason why that should not be consistent with anybody's view on the right to life It is certainly consistent with decency and humanity.
I should like to quote a colleague of mine who is no longer in the House but who is a well respected former member, Mrs. Grace Maclnnis, who spoke in the minority parliament on July 6, 1973, on this subject. This is what she said:
But like our own Dr. Morgentaler they have found themselves unable to wash their hands of the matter and piously leave women to suffer the tortures and dangers of a pregnancy which they did not want, for which they were only partly responsible, and which, in far too many cases, they did not know how to prevent.
This is the reality and the hyprocrisy of the whole matter of keeping abortion in the Criminal Code. This is where the injustice lies. I have tried to keep my remarks in low key, without touching on those horrors so often depicted graphically and in words when this matter is discussed.
I have tried to do that also. I do not think this very legitimate debate is enhanced with pictures of deceased women in morgues, or pictures of fetuses. I think that does nothing to rationalism in the debate. I respect views on the right to live and I recognize the concern that many people have that if life is taken, even in its growing form within the womb, if it is taken lightly we may have less respect for it. But there are no absolutes in this and women have a right not to be discriminated against in this one area where in vast parts of our country abortion is not available. Canada has one of the lowest abortion rates in the world. Those are things we should not forget.
Madam Speaker, I see my time is running out. However, I want to give credit to the Minister of Justice for one thing, that is that his position has apparently changed. In his latest memorandum of February 26, 1975, he departed very significantly from the position he had taken previously in advising hospitals, particularly those under his jurisdiction, that social and economic conditions were not to be considered in the decision whether to perform an abortion. In his last memorandum he stated:
For our part, it is clear that the justification for killing a fetus which parliament wrote into the law is one of health and life and that it is best to leave that judgement to experts. If medical committees will accept the responsibility and endeavour seriously to determine if the grounds set out by parliament are present, then the law will operate as intended.
I can live with that as a statement of the minister's responsibility. But it is a far, far cry from his conduct at the time when debate developed in the House between the minister and members of the opposition, when previous statements by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance were put to him. So I am pleased to
Abortion
see that there is a change. Nevertheless, it is a very deep responsibility that the Minister of Justice bears in the conduct of his office. During the period when he wrote the memorandum, when he attempted to stop grants to women's groups because of his suspicion that they may have been referring some of the women they were counselling to places where they could obtain abortions, there was an abuse of the minister's office, I submit.
We cannot use confidentiality to hide behind as a cloak with respect to what is fundamentally the government's responsibility, that is, to let the public know what has been happening on the abortion issue across the country and see how the Minister of Justice has been administering his portfolio. I urge, Madam Speaker, that the minister be required to table this correspondence so we can determine whether some of the things that I have read today are confirmation of the minister imposing his own interpretation of the Criminal Code on the attorneys general of this country.

Madam Speaker, I find it incongruous and infinitely sad that we should have listened to a speech in defence of somebody who is a self-admitted criminal. Dr. Morgentaler admitted that he had aborted women. The salient question he asked was whether they had enough money to pay him. These are the facts that came out in the transcript of the trial. Yet the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) is accused of hiding behind government confidentiality. We heard words such as "suspicion".
Questions such as whether the minister is carrying out his responsibility as Minister of Justice are being asked. Our Minister of Justice is being almost impeached in the House of Commons for carrying out his duty and defending the people of Canada. It is sad to see attempts at impeaching him when a known criminal is offered an award as a humanitarian. It may be a sign of what this society of ours is coming to. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star of Wednesday, May 28, under the title "Signals of social breakdown". It reads:
In Canada there's a growing fear of social and political breakdown ... The danger is that an individual may think he can disregard the rules he doesn't like, and get away with it. But when everyone-groups, organizations and unions-
And, I may add, abortionists.
-does the same, it's destructive to society as a whole.
I understand the role of the Minister of Justice. His role is to make sure that justice is administered to all Canadians, to all humans. I submit that humanity starts at the moment of conception. Therefore, I am convinced that the Minister of Justice would be remiss in his job if he did not protect the weakest. And what is weaker than an unborn child?
We have been told that Dr. Morgentaler had great courage. We have been told that our Minister of Justice has been hiding. I think the hon. member wanted to give the minister a chance to defend himself. Quite frankly, I know of no other minister in the present cabinet who has so ably and so often defended himself both in this House and

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext:
We are told that the Minister of Justice-I am quoting the hon. member-has a deep and sensitive responsibility to be humane. What is more humane than admitting that after 17 days blood cells are formed in a fetus; after 20 days the heart and primitive intestine are formed; after 24 days the heart begins to beat in a fetus? The fetus is weak and is dependent upon its mother. Is it not humane to protect that heart and to let it grow to its full maturity until birth which comes along after the proper gestation period? That is what our Minister of Justice has been trying to do. Now he is accused of being secretive and of hiding behind confidentiality. I think the minister deserves a tremendous vote of thanks from all Canadians. He is a pillar of our society.
The hon. member ended by giving some credit to the minister. Frankly, I am afraid I missed it. I was too appalled by the accusations and innuendos. I will not repeat myself, Madam Speaker. I know there are other people who want to speak on this subject and who are as incensed as I am that a man who is protecting the weakest element of our society is now being impeached in this chamber. If I may, I would like to quote part of the oath of Hippocrates;
The regimen I shall adopt shall be for the benefit of my patients according to my ability and judgment, and not for their hurt or for any wrong. I will give no deadly drug to any, though it be asked of me, nor will I counsel such, and especially I will not aid a woman to procure abortion.
The doctors who now brag of having broken our law took this oath. Do they now become heroes. Or is the real hero not the man who is being asked now to produce his papers?

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments in this most important debate. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and, as I anticipated, he referred to the definition of the World Health Organization. He made reference to previous comments by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) regarding health and his interpretation of it, and the hon. member discussed the law as interpreted now and in the past. He discussed the Morgentaler case and he reiterated the same arguments we have heard from him so many times in the past. He reiterated them on behalf of many other individuals who support the pro-abortionist movement.
I say to the hon. member that in my view he has not accurately assessed the changing mood of the people of Canada as they have become more knowledgeable about the realities of abortion and more vocal in their determination to stop abortion on demand. I think this has been demonstrated in two ways today in this House. The Committee of One Million in presenting their brief on abortion to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last week and in presenting their petition today to the House of Commons,

expressed their concern over the escalation of abortions which now exceed 43,000 per year in Canada, or 12.6 per cent of live births. They also expressed their concern regarding the deleterious effects of abortion on the health of women and their subsequent offspring, and about the social effects of widespread abortion in decreasing respect for every individual human life.
The formation of an all-party group in defence of the unborn child emphasizes the importance with which members of parliament view this problem and their earnest desire to promote fresh, meaningful debate. I believe the new order has begun. A new Canadian conscience is growing and demanding accurate information and informative debate, not only in this chamber but in every community and home in Canada. There is no place for misleading statements and misinformation which have contributed to the present situation of abortion on demand. The goal is to seek accurate information about the life and the world of the unborn child, to seek new approaches, to protect the life of the unborn child and to ensure that a mother's rights to health, happiness and freedom from other burdens are also protected.
I believe it is the responsibility of members of parliament to give the Canadian people the opportunity to determine the laws which will govern this country and it is in this spirit that I wish to make a few personal observations. The issue of abortion is not a private matter. It is not a sectarian religious problem or one of private morality. The issue is not to determine when life begins, for that is a scientific fact which is well known. The question which must be answered is what value we shall place on human life in general and whether the unborn human life in particular is entitled to legal protection.
The implications of this observation extend beyond the special concern of abortion, and in the final analysis they may be more important than the abortion issue before us. If we can justify the killing of an unborn child because it does not, by definition, fall within the arbitrary boundaries of humanity, then the question must logically be asked, will we decide that an individual, because of mental illness, senility, severe brain damage following an accident or for other reasons ceases to have the capability to lead a meaningful life, loses the protection of the law? The list of questions which can and should be asked in this regard is endless.
In the broader context of the abortion issue I would like to make reference to an editorial entitled, "A new ethic for medicine and society." This was published in the official journal of the California Medical Association at the height of a debate regarding the liberalization of the abortion law in California. The editorial discusses the controversy which exists not only in the United States but here as well in which the intrinsic worth and equality of every human life is secured by law regardless of age or health. It also discusses a new ethic according to which human life can be taken for what are viewed to be compelling social, economic or psychological needs of others. I would like to quote an important section of this article and it is as follows:
The process of eroding the old ethic and substituting the new has already begun. It may be seen most clearly in changing attitudes toward human abortion. In defiance of the long-held western ethic of intrinsic and equal value for human life regardless of its stage, condi-
May 29, 1975

tion, or status, abortion is becoming accepted by society as moral, right, and even necessary. It is worth noting that this shift in public attitude has affected the churches, the laws, and public policy rather than the reverse.
Since the old ethic has not yet been fully displaced, it has been necessary to separate the idea of abortion from the idea of killing, which continues to be socially abhorrent. The result has been a curious avoidance of the scientific fact, which everyone really knows, that human life begins at conception and is continuous whether intra or extra-uterine until death. The very considerable semantic gymnastics which are required to rationalize abortion as anything but taking a human life would be ludicrous if they were not often put forth under socially impeccable auspices. It is suggested that this schizophrenic sort of subterfuge is necessary because while a new ethic is being accepted the old one has not yet been rejected.
In defining a growing role of physicians in deciding who will and will not live, the editorial went on to state:
One may anticipate further development of these roles as the problems of birth control and birth selection are extended inevitably to death selection and death control whether by the individual or by society.
Those of us who believe in the old ethic, and I am convinced that represents by far the majority of Canadians, are looking to the political process to reflect these views.
It is extremely important in debating this issue that we work and seek a point of view which can be accepted by all rational men and women. In this regard I must say to my colleagues and those individuals who utilize the term "sanctity of life" that I find the term is restrictive. In many cases it may only be accepted by those with religious views. It does have the advantage, or disadvantage depending on the point of view, of settling the abortion debate. In similar fashion for those who have the points of view that support abortion on demand, the debate is settled very quickly. So I say to you, Madam Speaker, that it is impossible to have a meaningful dialogue with that term.
Another term which is frequently used and which has some credibility is "quality of life". I know that term is used very frequently by those to my left. I believe it is at times an overworked phrase and can take on a very serious dimension which is unacceptable to the majority of people. When quality of life is interpreted as abortion, when quality of life allows a deformed infant to die, or when quality of life determines whether government medical priorities infuse funds to the elderly rather than to the young-and I give that as an example-then surely it is obvious that a consensus among men and women will not be reached.
The question must then be asked: is there a common point of view acceptable to all? I believe the answer to that question is an unqualified yes. In Canada we have the Bill of Rights and in the United States the Constitution, which indicate that to be human is to possess certain rights, and among these is the right to life.
The phrase, the right to life, suggests something objective, something which can be defined and acted upon. For example, the fetus has a right to life; a comatose patient has a right to life; a patient with a brain stem injury who is in a coma has a right to life.
Abortion
This implies that a life should not be taken without adequate justification, and every living thing has a presumptuous right to live. In these circumstances the burden of proof rests on the individual who would take life and not on the individual who would preserve it. I recognize this leaves the crucial issue undetermined, namely, when is taking life justified? That, of course, is where disagreements occur.
I would state in the strongest terms possible that if we are looking for a point of view with universal acceptance, the right to life would fit the criterion, in my view. Such a point of view would protect our own self-interests and concern for our family, friends, and community. It is obvious there is an advantage to each of us to honour such a direction. And what is more important, Madam Speaker, it places the burden of proof on those who disobey the rule and opens the debate, as it should be opened, to decide what constitutes justifiable exceptions.
I hope my brief comments will serve a useful purpose in forming the framework upon which scientific data and the broad range of new knowledge and information can be added. I am convinced that if this House is permitted to debate this particular issue at a later date with honesty, with seriousness on the part of all members, and in a very rational form, and with new sources of information and knowledge, then the Committee of a Million that has been in Ottawa today will have been successful in its efforts.

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext:
It is a
rare event when we hear in this House a speech of such high principle and practical wisdom as we have just heard from an hon. member who is, I would remind you, Madam Speaker, a medical doctor.
I should like to say a word in response to the speech made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) who summed up his remarks by saying, "Let's find out what is happening in the abortion issue". I can tell the hon. member what is happening.
I want to make some remarks concerning the suggestion of the hon. member in a spirit that I hope he will accept-a spirit that is not contentious, not filled with wild emotion. I would ask him to look at this very serious question in a way that I know he is capable of looking at it. In the time that we have served together in this House I have to come to admire the hon. member for the perspicacity of his approach, for his fighting spirit, for his legal expertise. Because he possesses these qualities I would ask him to move to an even higher level in this question and consider the civil rights of the unborn child.
The hon. member put forward a case that has a fundamental flaw. When he was summing up that portion of his remarks regarding Dr. Morgentaler he was calling for more therapeutic abortion committees to permit the kind of abortions that he would like to see permitted in the country. He moved from that to what is his real purpose, the real approach that he brings to this House, and that is not so much that he wants more therapeutic abortions as that he wants abortion taken out of the Criminal Code and made a private matter between a woman and her doctor- a matter in which, as he says, women will not be discriminated against.
6254

May 29, 1975
Abortion
I want to go on to the legal position. I encourage the hon. member to review this. I say to him, as the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) has said, that abortion is not a private matter. The destruction of human life, even incipient or developing human life in the womb, can never be considered a private matter under our law.
I am not going to take the time to go down the side avenue of the legal case of a pregnant woman being hurt in an automobile accident and the double suit that results because there is a double life. I only want to say to the hon. member that just as the civil right to vote and the civil right against discrimination that all of us have must be protected by law, so too must the most fundamental and basic of civil rights, the right to life, be protected by law. It is that protection by law of the right of the unborn children of our country that I am addressing myself to, and practically no other element of this very complex issue.
If it was the intention of parliament to have the kind of abortion law envisaged by the hon. member for New Westminster, I think parliament would have made that clear in the 1969 amendments. I, too, have read those debates. I have come to the conclusion that it was not the intention of parliament to put through a law, the result of which would be the quadrupling of abortions over the next four years. In the year 1973, the most recent year for which statistics are available, there were 43,201 abortions, or 12.6 per cent of live births in this country.
I submit that the facts on that occasion illustrate the deep concern that members of parliament had to protect human life in the womb and at the same time to provide that avenue, as my colleague from Lambton-Kent said, for what constitutes justifiable exceptions. Therefore I appeal to the hon. member to consider that the intent of parliament, however badly that law was finally framed, was to protect human life and to allow for exceptions in cases that would be medically indisputable.
The hon. member comes from a province adjoining mine, the province of British Columbia. I ask him to consider British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario, the three wealthiest provinces in this country, which now have the highest rates of abortion by far. Are we to suspect that it is more dangerous to a woman's health to be pregnant in British Columbia, Alberta or Ontario than in any other province? Surely that fact alone illustrates that in those provinces abortions are being performed for social reasons, which was not the intent of parliament.
As legislators we must give very serious consideration to our responsibilities. A short while ago the hon. member and I were on the external affairs committee together. We achieved a result because there was collaboration. We achieved something that will benefit Canada in the long run. We did that by working together, even though we do not share the same basic views. I ask him whether we can work together, as reasonable people who have a common bond in this House, for good law. I cannot believe that the hon. member will accept any law as good if it violates the civil rights of unborn children in such escalation as we have seen over the past four years.

The hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) brought in a petition today with over one million names. I remember a cold, wintry day in November, 1973, when the Alliance for Life and associated groups came to parliament Hill with a petition of 350,000 names. They presented it to members of parliament in a demonstration of concern for the pro-life movement. We encouraged them to go back to their homes around the country and triple their efforts to bring back to parliament a petition containing the names of one million Canadians who wanted nothing more or less than justice on the abortion laws.
Today we have seen the result of the determination of that group of people who have touched the nerves of so many Canadians from coast to coast. The petition they brought in today asks members of parliament to consider this question seriously. Members of parliament from all four parties in this House have banded together in a spirit of co-operation to try to achieve a good law. I appeal to the minister and the hon. member for New Westminster to join with us.
We have produced a statement which all hon. members in this House are invited to join through signature or association. Many members of parliament have already become associated with this inter-parliamentary group. I predict that it is going to grow. As it grows and as we move into a major debate in this House, I ask the hon. member to consider seriously whether he can work with us to achieve what is our common goal of law.
The hon. member for York South put on record the words of the petition so that those thousands of Canadians who will be seeing Hansard over the course of the next few weeks will be familiar with what is actually stated in the petition. I want to put on record a few paragraphs of our statement of concern with which members of parliament are becoming associated. I quote the precise statement:
As members of parliament, representing all parties, we wish to indicate publicly our concern at the growing number of abortions in Canada.
Section 251 of the Criminal Code permits a therapeutic abortion committee to allow an abortion when continuation of a mother's pregnancy "would be likely to endanger her life or health". Since that law went into effect, abortions quadrupled to 43,201 in the four years 1970-73 and are now 12.6 per cent of live births in Canada.
This indicates to us that the word "health" is being defined very broadly and that in fact abortions are being permitted for a variety of social reasons. We believe parliament did not intend this to happen and we ask that legislative action now be taken to stop this needless escalation while at the same time allowing abortions in genuine cases of danger to life or health.
We affirm that abortion is not a private matter. The destruction of human life, even incipient or developing human life in the womb, can never be considered a private matter under our law. Nor is abortion a merely sectarian religious problem or one for the area of private morality. As legislators, we view abortion as a question of civil rights: the civil right to life of the unborn child. The civil rights of the mother cannot be expressed by summarily taking away the life of the unborn child.
In saying this we also emphasize our support of measures to assist pregnant women who are troubled. A positive response to social problems will help to remove the desire for abortion.
All this is a profound and delicate problem.
As legislators, we recognize that the problem must be dealt with primarily in parliament. It is not a matter of better application of the present law; it is the wording of the present law which permits such
May 29, 1975

loose application and which consequently must be changed. This issue, cutting to the very core of life itself, transcends partisanship, and it is in a spirit of collective responsibility that we are seeking a better law. To this end we have formed a Parliamentary Group in Defence of the Unborn.
We welcome the petition of one million signatures sponsored by the Committee of One Million which requests legislation "providing for the child conceived but not yet born the same protection provided for any other person."
We ask the Canadian government to give earnest consideration to a legislative change in Section 251 to restrict abortions to cases where the medical need is indisputable.
I close on this note. I believe this to be a moderate and responsible approach taken across the aisle of this House, and I ask the government to give serious consideration to what we have set forth in this document, one which expresses the will of one million Canadians and many more besides.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES ON SUBJECT OF ABORTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the important matter we are debating today concerns the confidential nature of the discussions and communications between the federal and the provincial governments. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) has asked that copy of the correspondence on abortion and section 251 of the Criminal Code exchanged between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), the provincial attorneys general and provincial health ministers be tabled in the House.
In the last few years, the disclosure of information by ministers of the Crown has been the subject of many a discussion. Indeed, on March 15, 1973, the President of the Privy Council proposed a series of guidelines on that vast subject. The correspondence concerned in the motion before the House obviously falls under section 4, which guarantees the confidentiality of government documents whose disclosure could be prejudicial to federal-provincial relations.
On presenting that text, the President of the Privy Council stated, and I quote:
Our objective is to make as much information available as possible. We believe that Members of Parliament require factual information about the operations of the government in order that they may carry out their parliamentary duties. That statement is included in the general principle. We are also aware that the desire to make available as much information as possible must be balanced against effective public administration, protection of the security of the state and rights to privacy. It is always a delicate matter of judgment to balance the desire to make information available with the effective administration of the government, security of the state and other considerations.
All members, I am convinced, recognize unreservedly the often delicate and extremely complex character of federal-provincial relations. It is obvious that in some cases, the first governmental objective-information- should give place to superior interests, of which free and honest communication between the federal and provincial governments is not the least. One cannot deny that when information is intended for the population or for public debate, its expression often takes on a meaning or colour that is different from that which is important to the promotion and preservation of elements of compromise and comprehension as well as to the openness of mind and equilibrium essential to federal-provincial relations. It seems to me, Madam Speaker, that this touches on the
Committee Report
main principles governing the divulging of internal administrative instructions and documents.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, may I point out that the Minister of Justice, members of parliament and the public in general have all interest in any information on governmental activities being published, but obviously, in my statement, there must be "reasonable" limits to such a policy, and the word "reasonable" is the key word, so that the government may act with efficiency and security. As a result, the exclusion of intergovernmental correspondence, such as the kind mentioned in the motion, represents an exception that is motivated as well as essential. In the present case, Madam Speaker, official secret regulations have been well observed, of that I am convinced, so I would ask the hon. member to withdraw his motion. Madam Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-16, to amend certain statutes to provide equality of status thereunder for male and female persons, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned at five o'clock I was mentioning that in the old days female employees could be laid off because they were pregnant or after giving birth. This practically never happens nowadays, neither among federal employees who are not civil servants nor even in the private sector. So the legislation has evolved. Representations were made to that effect by organizations which defended the role of women in business, and employers took heed.
Mr. Speaker, there is also in that omnibus bill an amendment which caught my attention and which I fully endorse. I am referring to the cadet corps sponsored by the National Defence Department. Up to now, that department only accepted young boys in that cadet corps, and in the amendment of the minister, the word "person" would be substituted for "boy", which would enable young girls to take an active part in such cadet corps. Now, there again, Mr. Speaker, even though it was not provided in the act, the Department of National Defence has been allowing young girls into cadet corps for at least two years. In fact, a few days ago, I attended in La Sarre, in my constituency, the tenth anniversary of the foundation of the cadet corps, and I noticed several young girls among the cadets. At the various information booths, we saw for ourselves that those young girls, especially in the field of communications, managed quite well among the boys of that cadet corps. They showed that they could provide us with the required information, that they could find co-ordinates on maps of the area and, therefore, eventually render services and even direct, if necessary, the operations of a military corps. Well, I agree with that provision of Bill C-16 which will actually allow young girls to enrol in those cadet corps. Since it was decided that 1975 would be Women's Year in Canada, the press especially and the broadcasting media have given that event a wide coverage. This publicity has not always turned out to women's advantage. Even if they wanted or thought they would liberate women in all their daily activities or whatever, it seems that they tried to ridicule the role of women at home, and it is quite unfortunate. They have tried to lead people to believe that women had no future at home, that they should be only outside, that they could be useful only out of their home, which I believe, Mr. Speaker, is completely wrong.
Recently in northwest Quebec, in Abitibi, there has been a meeting of more than 250 women from Abitibi, a meeting

about a project for the promotion of women; the women at the meeting have been able during that day to evaluate their situation and to think over many aspects of life today. They believe that publicity diminishes women by leading people to believe that the mother or the wife at home is of no use to society. They suggested that women at home bring out human values, they prepare the society of tomorrow, first by giving life, by educating children, by giving them the sense of moral and social responsibilities, as the family is the cell of society.
Mr. Speaker, how often have we seen or heard judges of the social welfare court mention that juvenile delinquency, for example, was generally due to the desertion of women from home. They have deplored this situation. But, to try through a huge and well-organized campaign to make people believe that a woman's place is not at home anymore, that is fostering juvenile delinquency. A woman's duty is first and foremost to her-home. When she has to work outside for long hours, especially when there are young children, she cannot achieve maximum efficiency, either in one place or the other.
There is another important role: that played by a woman within the family. There is no better way to get involved in society. As far as religion is concerned, it is emphasized that the woman who believes in Christ gives another dimension to moral and human values; she gets involved in a more serene manner. That also is important, Mr. Speaker. There is too much of a tendency nowadays to forget human values. This definitely leads us to lose the sense authority. In the last fifteen years, especially in Quebec, there has been constant demands to relax authority, so that next to nothing is respected anymore. There is no more respect for authority. Parental authority is disregarded. So is government authority, at every level. The law is ignored, so we should not wonder at what is now happening. This is important. We must insist that the woman with small children may spend all her time bringing up her children, if she so desires. Ten years ago or so, one bank researched the homemaker's monetary value, what should be a fair return for the work she does in the home. The figure was quite impressive.
This is what was found ten years ago. The daily work load of the wife was assessed as follows: As a baby-sitter, $55.63 a week; as a dietitian, $3 a week; as a shopper, $4.95; as a cook, $32.75; as a dishwasher, $9.30; as a housekeeper, $26.25; as a washerwoman, $11.21; as a seamstress, $3.25; as a practical nurse, $1.20; as a caretaker, $3.83; as a gardener, $3.57; as a driver, $4.44 a week. That makes a total of $159.38, and that was ten years ago.
Mr. Speaker, if we had to pay wives at those rates, I believe that many more men would wash dishes, do the housework and the shopping, but such is not the case. The fact is that the housewife plays a very important role which frees the husband and enables him to spend more time at his work and earn what is required to support this cell of society that is the family.
Mr. Speaker, these values must not be ignored. This is why we are always trying to improve our social legislation, for instance. When we press the government, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde),
May 29, 1975

for instance, we are often thought hard to deal with and demanding, but, Mr. Speaker, we do this precisely to give more freedom to women, to enable the wife with young children to do her work and raise her children without having to get outside work in order to supplement the income required for the welfare of her family.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that Bill C-16, which includes several amendments, will improve in certain cases the status of women. In other cases, it may deprive the wife of certain privileges she previously had, for instance, when her husband is brought before the court for a criminal offence. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this bill should be considered further in the appropriate committee, and I believe that for the moment, even though we could ask for more, either in this bill or in the related legislation, it remains an important step, and we are ready to support and endorse it.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the feminist author Simone de Beauvoir said that there were two kinds of beings in this world, human beings and women, but that when women began behaving like human beings they were accused of trying to be like men. We've come a long way as the ads say, but we have a whole world of attitudes to change before we will progress much further.
It was in 1921 that Agnes MacPhail blazed a trail from the prairies to Parliament Hill. But even then, once we knew the way, we did not follow in large numbers. In 1972 there were five women in this chamber. The persisting myths and fables about women must be banished forever. We women are reputed to be waspish, ungenerous, even evil; and of course, most of all, we are reputed to hate each other. We are manipulated to oppose each other like prize cats, a tactic that has worn thin with age and fatigue, for women of every station in life, of every philosophical persuasion, have come to realize that by being supportive of each other, by giving the other woman the edge, if you will, the unity that results can change our destinies.

speechtext:
You will find that 34 per cent of families are headed by women in this country today. Is raising children to become exclusively women's work? I have real faith that the new generation will reserve this trend and allow fathers who wish it to become an integral part of their children's lives.
One of the concerns of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), both as minister of that department and as minister responsible for the status of women, has been to study the possibility of including non-wage earning spouses, those who work in the home, under the Canada Pension Plan. It was for this reason that last year he requested the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Committee to submit proposals to him, outlining ways in which spouses who work in the home could become contributors to the Canada Pension Plan. Early this year he received the recommendations of these two groups.
Both advisory bodies considered three alternatives unacceptable. They concluded that it would be impractical to include non-wage earning spouses in the plan through the payment of a salary to spouses working at home. In addition, they submitted recommendations against including spouses in the plan through a system of voluntary contributions or through the establishment of a separate plan.
They did both recommend, however, that spouses at home be included within the plan, and that Canada Pension Plan credits be evenly divided or split between marriage partners for the purpose of applying benefits and other provisions-either on a continuing basis, or only in case of marriage breakdown. The Canada Pension Plan Advisory Committee suggested that this might be carried out on a universal basis, or only in the case of marriage breakdown. The ACSW, on the other hand, proposed that the splitting of credits be implemented on a universal basis for the future and, in the case of marriage breakdown, splitting of past pension credits also.
Now let us look for a moment at that romantic stereotype with which we are all so familiar, marriage. You all know it well. Women and men are socialized to believe that their roles as mother and wife and father and husband will prove to be the ultimate source of fulfillment. In some cases blessed couples are able to accomplish that, but the realities of marriage are harsh.
Let us look at some marriage laws and interpret the meaning, clear eyed and without romance, as a recent women's publication did. Here we have what women think about marriage:
The law says a husband must support his wife and children ... but a working wife can keep all her earnings for herself. She does not have to support her husband or even her children. The law means women are not responsible for supporting other people, women are kept, they are not keepers. The law says the wife must live wherever the husband chooses. If she doesn't she can be classified as a deserting wife. She will lose her dower rights and right to support, and he can divorce her. The law means she must be physically available. The law says if the wife leaves the husband or is unfaithful to him, she loses her right to be supported by him and she loses her right to his property. The law means even if she has lived with him for 20 years and has been a full-time cook, housekeeper, nursery-maid, janitor, secretary and lover, all without pay, she loses her rights to everything as soon as she stops
[Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).j
providing sexual services exclusively for him. The wife has a right to the husband's property only so long as she is part of his property. The law says the husband can sue for loss of consortium, the wife cannot. The law means the wife has pledged her body, the husband has not... The law says a man cannot be convicted of rape if the victim is his wife. The law means it is not a crime to violate what you own.
There was talk of urgency today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), and he is right. There is urgency. Women have defined beyond question their needs; they have been studied, they have been analysed, they have been researched. Now is the time to end the study and the talk, now is the time for action. Women have sought out their history and their heroines, and there are many, many heroines in this country, ordinary Canadian women who have striven, worked, protected, comforted and nurtured their families but who have sought a richer, kinder, gentler life for all mankind at the same time. Kindness is our weapon and our strength. A society as torn with extremes as ours requires healthy doses of love, warmth, and kindness if it is to survive. But we want these to be considered and actually to be male as well as female attributes. We want these characteristics to be assumed unashamedly.

In other words, we want both sexes to be full-flowering, well-rounded, loving human beings.
"Vive la vie", I see it around me today everywhere. Life is sacred and precious, and I agree most fervently. But "vive la vie" must be considered at both extremes in our society and in our time, and I submit that in extreme circumstances there will be abortions and there will be capital punishment under the laws as they presently stand. The two are irretrievably locked in logic. Neither abortion nor capital punishment would take place in an enlightened society. Abortion should be unnecessary, execution by the state unwarranted. But sadly, in my opinion, we are not at that stage of development at this time.
Before I was elected I told my future constituents how I felt about the issue of abortion. I said I believed abortion should be removed from the Criminal Code and placed under the provisions of the National Health Act.
I believe there are considerably more abortions taking place in our hospitals than are necessary, and I submit these abortions are dehumanizing to women and weaken their general integrity. I do not think that hospital committees are functioning in the manner in which they were intended to function in some cases, and I do not think the present system is equally administered across the country.
I believe that checks and balances are required, and I respect the stand of the Alliance for Life, but unfortunately L cannot agree with them, because until our country places more emphasis on sexual responsibility and contraception, there will continue to be too many abortions. There have always been abortions, there are abortions now, and I submit that until we have a perfect society there will continue to be abortions.
If we submit to the anti-abortionists, there will resume in our back streets the devastating disgrace of illegal abortions, a return to the maiming and deaths of women in the past. On the other hand, if we move to the completely pro-abortion stand, we will do irreparable harm to the
May 29, 1975

social fabric of this nation. The Hippocratic oath, I submit, would have been written differently in the matter of abortion had it been men who conceived in ancient Athens!
It has been an emotional day in the House and many of us have met with the earnest representatives of the Alliance for Life, but I appeal to members of the House, and to people outside this House who look to us for leadership, for a rational approach to a profoundly complex problem. The present law of the land is a good law when administered with equity.
I think I would like to answer one question that was raised by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). He wondered why the richest provinces had the highest abortion rate. I can offer an answer to the hon. member. The answer is that the wealthy of this country and the wealthy of the world have always had access to abortion, and the poor, the ill-educated, and those who are unfortunate not to share our level of life, have not. Their sisters are beginning to have the same type of equity as has been known in the circles of the rich since time began.
There must always be room for rational thought. Slides of aborted fetuses to sensationalize a particular philosophy serve no other purpose than to bring to mind the revolting human degradation of women who were driven by such desperation as most men cannot imagine to attempt to abort themselves, or to submit their bodies to an inept, illegal, back-street abortionist. Is the bloody and dismembered fetus any more or less repugnant to anyone here to view than, for instance, a thirteen year old girl, crouched naked in death in her own blood, after attempting to abort herself with a sharpened kitchen implement? I leave those two thoughts in the minds of hon. members tonight as they consider the status of women in this nation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that although perhaps some of us in the House would not agree completely with all of the sentiments that have been expressed by the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo)-and I emphasize "the hon. member"-there are none in the House who would in any way deny the conviction and passion with which her speech to us was delivered this evening. After having said that, I would like to deal with the basis of the bill, and not to deny in any way the very strong feelings which the hon. member for Skeena has expressed.
Some time ago the director of the Women's Bureau of the Department of Labour was speaking at Thunder Bay, Ontario, and she put forward in a very simple but a very profound way the principle that the bill seeks to advance. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote her words on that particular occasion so that they may appear in the records of the House. She said:
Canadian society consists of a single total entity made up of many component parts, men and women comprising the two basic major components. But men and women in Canadian society belong to a considerable number of cultural, ethnic and religious groups, each of which is in itself an integral component of the total social structure.
Status of Women
Only in recent years have we come to understand that the quality of this total society cannot be higher than the quality of the least advantaged of all of its components. Thus, if the status of any one ethnic group is of a lower degree than that of another ethnic group, the quality of the total Canadian society is reduced, if the status of one cultural group is considered to be inferior to that of another, then the quality of the total Canadian cultural mosaic is thereby lowered. If the status of one racial group is inferior to that of another, then the quality of the total Canadian society is lessened.
Similarly, if the status of women in Canadian society is less than that of men, either in law or in practice-
As was so well put by the hon. member for Skeena.
-then the status of Canadian society, as a whole, is lowered thereby. For in these circumstances Canada is not only seen to be a society in which evenhanded justice fails to prevail but the country is deprived of one of its greatest resources, for it is deprived of a potential inherent in half of the population.
I think that hon. members on all sides of this House will agree that the words of the speaker on that occasion were indeed profound.
If Bill C-16 is carefully reviewed it can be found that it is part of the legislative action we must deal with in this House if we are to give more than lip service to the sound principle which is being discussed tonight, the principle of equality of status. In speaking to this bill and in stating my basic support for what it contains, I want to make it clear that I do not condone what must be described, even by the most unbiased observer, as some pretty slow progress by the government.
This bill, or one similar to it, was introduced into the twenty-ninth parliament, but during those days the government was more concerned with survival than with equity and justice, so it was allowed to die. I believe that its action-or in this case, its lack of action-is more eloquent than ministerial protestation and pronouncements, particularly in that year which preceded International Women's Year. This lack of action, I submit, speaks for itself. The fact is that the government has given a low priority to the status of women in our society.
In the fall of 1974 the bill came forward again in the form in which it is now before us, and here we are halfway through International Women's Year, just beginning the discussion of the principles of this bill, and at a time when this House is running into the tail end of the first half of this session. And all of this is occurring in the atmosphere which was created by a minister who tried to give the impression on the program entitled "Lady is a Four Letter Word" that his government gave it a high priority.
In view of the atmosphere he tried to create, perhaps we may be able to thank the minister for saying what he did because I am convinced that if he had not been cornered on that program, thereby creating the impression that he did, he would not have had to move at long last. The minister has now moved, and I suggest with the greatest of respect to him that he has moved in this direction not out of any great commitment to the rights of women, but by reason of a great commitment to himself and his own preservation.

speechtext:
-because this piece of legislation does involve the fundamental rights of one-half of the Canadian people, how that one-half is to be treated, dealt with and considered, and in what way and whether that one-half is to be subject to the same law and the same practice as the other half.
What is the cause of women in Canada this year and, indeed, in every year to follow? Women in Canada are asking for the opportunity to play a full and complete role in the social, economic, and political life of this land. They ask for no more, and they will accept no less. In those terms they are asking all Canadians, men and women, to re-examine their respective attitudes toward women, and we are asked today to approve in principle a bill to give at least part of that re-examination some life.
I know of no case which could be based on a stronger foundation. Surely there are few causes which can claim to be based on such principles of human rights as have been proclaimed and are supported in our own country and in other countries throughout the world, through the auspices of the United Nations.
In Canada the fundamental document is the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, and human rights legislation, such as it is, in our statutes and in those of the provinces which have made advances in that sense. This bill puts forward for consideration by this House some eleven more of the recommendations of that royal commission, so it is important on that ground alone. But let us not rest on our oars, for this bill does not bring us to the end of our labours or to the end of the road. However, we can say that it is a step, even though it is a minuscule step, along the way to what women and, I hope, fairminded Canadians regardless of sex would like to see for that one-half of the population.
I had intended to deal at some length with the principles of the legislation. The minister was kind enough to do that in the course of his speech, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has also touched on it. The Committee will have an opportunity to deal with the detail of this legislation, so I will not do so at this time. Regardless of that, the changes which are inherent and understood in this legislation are long overdue.
Although some may say that the government and the minister cannot be faulted for bringing these changes forward at this time, I say with a great deal of respect for the minister that he and the government can certainly be faulted for not bringing them forward at an earlier stage in this parliament or, indeed, in the twenty-ninth parliament.
In considering this bill I think it is fair to say to the minister that the work of the government and of this parliament with respect to the position of women in our society and their status in that society is by no means completed. For example, I would call the attention of my

hon. colleagues to the position of women in the Public Service of Canada. Within that public service women are gaining some recognition for their abilities, but though women represent more than one third of the labour force they are still mainly restricted to lower paid, non management jobs. This is not to say that the onus must fall completely on the government. The government has made some efforts in the direction of assisting women, or providing the vehicle by which women can move into management positions to a greater degree.
There is certainly an onus on women to prepare themselves educationally for the positions they desire and then to push for recognition to obtain those positions. There is support for this from the Public Service Alliance of Canada, and I know that there is the same degree of support from the Professional Institute of the Public Service. I hope that as time goes on, women for their own part will adopt a firmer stand within their respective bargaining agencies. One would hope to see more women elected to executive positions in those bargaining agencies. I think that would be carrying on the example set by Mrs. Carr and others in the labour movement.
I suppose part of the problem is the question of attitude. I know the position is changing, but for many women now in the public service I am sure their early life was one in which they were encouraged to become participants in traditional women's occupations. There were likely very few Canadian homes in which it was said to the daughters of those homes that they ought to become lawyers, doctors, engineers, architects. This attitude is certainly changing as enrolment in the professional schools would indicate, but there is still that reluctance which only time and new attitudes can eliminate.
I would not want anyone to have the impression that the onus is all on the women in the work force to improve themselves-there is a very heavy onus on the men in the work force with respect to their attitude toward their employees who are women.
I should like to commend to members on all sides of the House an article, actually the first five articles, referred to by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. The title of the article is "Canadian Business Isn't Really Committed to Extending Equal Opportunity to Women". The findings of a survey done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of some 850 CBC women across Canada are surprising, to say the least.
The conclusions of the task force report are that the majority of women are dissatisfied with their status in the corporation; that they suffer from frustration in their work situation, and there is a growing feeling of powerlessness.
The very interesting statistic to be noted, and this was referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, is that the working environment in careers of CBC women are controlled by a male majority of three to one, who held an even greater proportion of decision-making power, 93 per cent of managerial jobs, and whose underlying beliefs about women's appropriate role at work differed drastically from the women's view of themselves. Another important finding is that there is a deepening frustration that
May 29, 1975

there had been so little change made. As well, there was a deep-seated belief that men were basically oblivious to their dissatisfaction and concerns, and had no real inclination toward equality of opportunity.
The results of all this, according to the report, are a reduced willingness to work, diminished productivity, and subtle forms of non co-operation in daily activities.
The report contained an excellent discussion on the problem as it relates to one corporation. I would respectfully commend it to members of the House because it concerned a public corporation analogous to the Public Service of Canada.
I would not want it to be said that there has been no advancement at all in terms of the public service. In fact the Public Service Commission annual report for 1974 does reveal some improvement in the statistical sense. But in the sense of the numbers of women involved in positions of increasing responsibility, the record is nothing to write home about. It is in this latter sense, as opposed to pure statistics, that progress should be measured.
One of the basic and classic cases of the lack of awareness of the government, and its failure to act with dispatch in terms of a large group of public servants, can be found in the case of the public service secretary and-the whole matter of rug-ranking. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I raised this matter in the House. It struck me as rather strange that the government, having received a brief in July, 1973, was only brought to a realization of the problem on February 14, 1974, a cold and frigid day when some thousands of public servants marched to this hill. For the first time there was a statement by the then minister responsible for the status of women, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), that he at least recognized that they had a problem. This was a victory won by the women in the public service by way of a peaceful demonstration.
There has been a lack of action, Mr. Speaker, and a lack of awareness, and these can be found in both the public and the private sector in the world of work. The fact is that women can no longer be restricted to traditional roles. The atmosphere and the circumstances must be provided that will enable them to make choices where they are encouraged to develop their own talents in any area that they choose. That principle ought to apply in the field of federal appointments-to the bench and to government boards and agencies, and to the Senate. In terms of the public service, of course, equal opportunity for women is more fundamental than that of merely filling posts at the top; it is at the middle and the lower echelons of the public service that there exist grave disparities between the numbers of men and women.
There is a tremendous requirement in all of the urban communities in Canada for the facility of properly staffed and properly equipped day care centres. There are some who regret the necessity for this kind of centre in the community, and they are entitled to their point of view. But social and economic conditions exist in this country where, to neglect day care facilities and their importance, can result in the imposition of an economic ball and chain to those women who choose, through necessity or otherwise, to enter the work force. There is a corresponding danger to the children of those women in terms of their care. The statistical parameters of the problem can be
Status of Women
simply put. In the city of Toronto there are 82,800 children in single parent families where there is the necessity for the parent to work.
We can deal with a number of factors that affect the status of women which this bill is intended to advance which, if I may put the case simply, is this. The case of women in Canada is the case of for equality before the law; equality in political life; in social and domestic life; education; and in employment.
While there is great emphasis given to the woman in the field of work, we must not forget those women who make the free choice of not participating in the work force but choose freely to participate in the community in the role of wife and mother. The government of Ontario has made some signal strides in this direction. The Law Reform Commission of the province of Ontario and the Attorney General of that province are to be congratulated. I suggest that such steps within the federal sphere would be welcome as well.
I do not know how one can reasonably argue that a woman who chooses to stay at home, raise children, and provide an atmosphere of tranquility, peace and stability, does not make a contribution in an economic sense to the well-being of that family unit and to the betterment of Canadian Society. Certainly the laws of contracts, and property rights, ought to recognize that equality. I believe that the law is generally moving in that direction.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say I do not believe that we have yet seen in this country or in the western hemisphere the opportunity for women, as one-half of the population of our country and of this hemisphere, to develop themselves fully in the sense that I have put before this House. I am one who firmly believes that while the initiative must rest with women to further their participation in those aspects of Canadian life, there is a duty on all Canadians, and a particular duty on this parliament and this government, to provide the atmosphere and the legislative framework for the advances that every fair-minded Canadian believes are right and just. Mr. Speaker, it is in that spirit that we must approach this legislation.
