Mr. Speaker, if at all times it has been said and readily recognized that behind every great man there stood a woman, I feel that the Progressive Conservatives, and especially the hon. member who has just spoken, should understand that the Liberals have learnt that lesson long ago and stick to it. The Liberal party has close to ten women members, whereas they have only one.
Another point raised by my colleague is that the government should appoint a great number of women to positions other than that of simply presiding over the Senate, but he did not say so clearly. I must remind him that in the past five years, seven Canadian women were appointed either to the Supreme Court of Canada or to the higher courts in the land. These are simply remarks that I wished to make following his speech which did not contribute much of anything positive.
But the fact remains that I realize, as he does, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian women have had to wait a long

May 29, 1975
Status of Women
time before obtaining true recognition. One has only to recall the few following facts. In 1858, women were allowed for the first time to attend lectures at the University of Sackville in New Brunswick, where not until 1867 were they allowed to take a university course, although without hope of obtaining a diploma. In 1879, the University of King's College granted its first B.A. to a woman. Only in 1884 did McGill admit women, and only in 1885 in the case of the University of Toronto.
As for the role of Canadian women in politics, we had to wait until 1876 for the emergence of the first suffragette associations organized in Toronto by Mrs. Emily Howard Stowe, the first ever women doctor in Canada, who was to advocate women's associations that rapidly spread throughout the country. Then in 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919, the provinces successively granted women the right to vote and to sit as members of parliament.
In the province of Quebec, which I represent, such rights were granted only in 1940, unfortunately. Only in 1957 did we have the first woman appointed Minister of the federal government.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, in 1975, while people of all countries are maximizing their efforts to eliminate all forms of segregation, our attitudes in our own country, which are based upon our deepest traditions, are prompting us against our will, I believe, to cultivate the least excusable form of discrimination towards the ones who, for a long time now, have shown us their equality pre-eminently, and I mean women with a capital "W".
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, one needs only take a look at a few recent statistics to show that before 1960, particularly in Quebec, people were talking about the elite from colleges and universities. But already in 1952, 21 per cent of registrations in colleges and universities were from women and that proportion reached 36 per cent in 1971-72. Moreover, I believe, whatever people may say, that liberal professions and professions from "social democracy", as some would say, were always the ones to contribute more than others to the progress of our societies. One has but to quote a few statistics to show to what degree women paved a way for themselves in our present society.
I need only talk about self-sacrifice. Whenever I talk about self-sacrifice, I talk about nurses. In 1968, 100 per cent of the nurses in Quebec were women. As regards social workers, 95 per cent were women. Twenty-two per cent of the psychologists were women although it is a science where it is most difficult to get a university diploma. I am also speaking about psycho-analysts and public relations agents.
I think we men must recognize that we have entertained and fostered certain myths because in 1968 .1 of 1 per cent of engineers were women. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is important that we change our attitude. As the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) mentioned both in this House and in interviews he had previously, the government may bring in any possible and imaginable legislation, but if the attitude of Canadians does not change, if we are not prepared to evolve, none of those pieces of legislation will bring the results hoped for.
Yet Canada, even if we blame ourselves, as early as 1972 and 1971, to contradict somewhat my colleague opposite,

passed an order in council to urge all deputy ministers to review the role of women within departments to make it easier for them to have access to senior positions in the public service. And in 1972, again Canada showed leadership at the international level-leadership that is increasingly recognized-by asking and putting before the International Labour Organization the instrument of ratification of Agreement No. 100 concerning equal pay for men and women for equal work.
Following the recommendations by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the government also quickly passed several measures both regulatory and legislative, and I mentioned one a few minutes ago. And in 1971 also under the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Liberal government passed a legislation providing a maternity leave of 17 weeks. And Bill C-16 that will be passed I am sure by the majority of those who have an enlightened mind, will be a step forward even though it may not be the ultimate end of the purposes the government intends to achieve.
Indeed, Bill C-16 contains excellent steps such as those that were pointed out by the Minister'of National Health and Welfare. He talked about the Canada Elections Act and the Criminal Code. However, there again perhaps women are losing some of their privileges. But actually, it is a sign of her equality when there is talk of complicity vis-a-vis her husband in respect of the Immigration Act, the Public Service Employment Act, pensions, the Veterans Pensions' Act and, as I said, the legislation of 1971.
All those actions are a step forward indeed. But there are others to be taken. When we talk about confinement leave, Madam Speaker, I think we should progress further. Just think of a Scandinavian country where women are granted-and that might be a measure to consider-six months' leave after confinement, and men are also granted six months' leave directly after that so that they can become thoroughly acquainted with the realities of home.
As far as industry is concerned, Madam Speaker, I think women, although they are reaching higher and higher, should make their way to executive occupations. In my profession, in lawyers' offices, I deeply regret that, when one of my colleagues who had completed her course applied at a lawyer's office, they would wonder why they would place hopes in a woman who, four or five years later, would get married, have a child, and leave the office. If that very conservative branch does not alter its attitude, as I mentioned earlier, we shall miss the boat. In the business world, in the financial world and in international relations, I met women who indeed could have given remarkable lessons to men who indulge in a conservatism which only women will reverse and turn into a better attitude.
Unfortunately, Madam Speaker, the year 1975 which was called Women's Year is falling short of its target, for this year should have been dedicated to the identification, not revalorization of women, since they were in Quebec and in Canada as a whole, I believe, given fair recognition. However, this year was used, I believe, more to voice claims than to identify women. The Secretary of State Department, through all its programs, gave Canadian women the opportunity to have programs which would enable them to come forward and display their sense of originality, not prove it, but show their mettle, for I think
May 29, 1975

it had already been proven. And I wonder, after talking with many women in my riding, whether some of the movements really are representative. Indeed, they served all sorts of more or less bitter purposes which only lead to recriminations. Women in the Chambly constituency like all other women in Quebec and the rest of Canada really want to live Women's Year in a better way than several associations let us know, and they really want to secure through this year's programs, the means of putting forward on a long term basis programs which will not only provide women in Canada with a better situation, but will enable us to reach that just society the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) advocated in 1968. And if a majority of our population are women, we must also expect great efforts on their part to help us govern this country. Just as the prime minister repeated in Montreal last weekend, to govern is not merely to pass pieces of legislation, it is to try to improve the condition of a whole society and that improved condition, Madam Speaker, is for both women and men and for the entire society, present and future.
Madam Speaker, I must congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who, I believe, increased his efforts by sponsoring Bill C-16. I commend him also for the meetings be held, for his drive and for the examples he gave to the Canadian people. It is not enough to pass laws in order that women be better accepted in the public service. It is not enough to pass laws in order to change something in immigration. It is necessary to adopt measures that will really change this society. Problems sometimes come from the laws, and I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare has already thought of a solution. I am also convinced that he has already engaged in talks with the provincial governments on that subject. One has only to think of the problem of alimonies when a woman wants to get a divorce. How many women are forced to collect their alimonies at unimaginable places. Their husband has fled the country, simply seeking to evade his obligations. I think the government must take steps to correct that situation. I remember that during the last electoral campaign, the Liberal party talked about a guaranteed income for all heads of families, and I expect this will be a subsequent step to Bill C-16.
Madam Speaker, we could enlarge upon many other subjects that should be dealt with along with Bill C-16, on the occasion of Women's Year. I believe hon. members who preceded me dealt with the proper subjects. As member of Parliament for Chambly, I wished to provide my whole support and agreement to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, to support the women and even the men who are participating in this year's activities and indeed urge them to understand the real meaning of Women's Year, instead of seeing in it a year in which we are merely going to display past sores without introducing new solutions.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset may I say we have heard several erudite speeches this evening and these have dealt well with the philosophical and ideological implications of Bill C-16. I should like to take a few minutes to deal with a number of practicalities and suggest ways of solving certain problems. Along with my party in general, I support this omnibus bill
Status of Women
which appears to be an attempt to provide equality of status as between males and females in our society.
I should like to make a few comments about the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act as applied to maternity cases, and the manner in which benefits are given out. I might say I question whether this omnibus bill is the appropriate place for these amendments. Successive ministers in this government have promised to bring in amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971. It appears they have failed to produce them because undoubtedly they were afraid of being defeated in the House. Again, they have talked about amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and there certainly is a need for a whole series of them. They were to have been brought in some time ago, but there is still little evidence that the government intends to move in this direction.
The cost of maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act is one which remains approximately the same from year to year. In 1973, according to the Unemployment Insurance Advisory Committee, almost $67 million were expended in benefits. Certainly maternity benefits do not rise or fall with unemployment rates to nearly the same extent as regular benefits. It is interesting to me that sickness benefits paid out in 1973 amounted to a little more than $80 million.
The proposed changes are, indeed, welcomed. The records of the committee studying the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 show that the need for these changes was brought to the attention of the minister at that time. The answer then was that the requirement concerning the eight weeks previous to the confinement and the seven weeks after the confinement was in keeping with established international labour legislation. I would be interested to hear whether this international legislation has taken a different course, or whether there is new thinking on these matters.
Eligibility to receive maternity benefits under the act rests, first of all, upon the ability to provide a medical certificate. This would, presumably, not create any difficulty for most people, but there might be a few cases in isolated areas where pre-natal care is carried out by medical personnel who do not hold medical degrees, and in such circumstances it might be difficult to get such a certificate easily. I hope provision will be made in the regulations to take care of any hardship cases which might arise.
The second criterion of eligibility requires the applicant to have worked for at least 20 weeks within the year preceding the claim or since the last unemployment insurance claim. This is at variance with the regular benefits which may be obtained after only eight weeks of regular employment. The 20-week stipulation is in line, I believe, with the sickness provision, but it does create significant problems for claimants if they get caught in certain anomalous positions. For instance, if a woman temporarily collecting unemployment benefits becomes pregnant and then finds work but is unable to continue so as to accumulate 20 weeks of employment, because of her pregnancy she will not be eligible for any benefits even though she is a permanent member of the work force and a bona fide working person. I do not know what might be done in cases such as this, but possibly a careful framing of the

May 29, 1975
Status of Women
regulations might be of help. I should like to hear from the minister on this point; we should certainly look carefully at this aspect in committee so that untoward hardship may be avoided.
Again, difficulties might arise in cases where a woman is an active member of the labour force at the time of conception. Human nature being what it is, few women remember precisely when they became pregnant, and as the months go by they become even more hazy as to when conception occurred. Most rule of thumb methods used to identify this date are based upon the date of the woman's last menstrual period. However, this is not a reliable guide due to the extreme variations in the physiological activities of women.
Most full time pregnancies are considered to last approximately 280 days, but again there seem to be wide variations. There is the celebrated case in English jurisprudence in which, in a paternity suit, the court accepted a gestation period of well over 300 days. Therefore the regulations governing the eligibility of maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act should be looked at carefully to prevent situations arising which will deprive people of their benefits through peculiar circumstances.
Further, in the pay-out of benefits considerable difficulty arises for recipients of maternity benefits. Pamphlets underline the fact to the recipient that "Your benefit payments begin after you have served the required two week waiting period". This statement is not only misleading but somewhat fallacious. Eligibility begins after a two week waiting period, but payment will not be received until five to seven weeks after the applicant's interruption of earnings. Nowhere is this fact documented and, as a result, many families budget on the expectation that they will be receiving benefit payments two weeks after application.
In other words, a single parent family, or family with no visible income outside that of the woman's, may go for up to two months without receiving any benefits or any income. The only alternative is welfare. However, when UIC benefits are viewed as insurance and a "right", as the government proclaims, this is really a poor alternative.
In this area the government might consider whether the waiting period prior to receiving benefits could be speeded up. Certainly there are individual cases where, if the mother were the only wage earner in the family and were closely tied to her work for necessary income, she would suffer considerably. A change of the benefit period, which is something that I mentioned as being deficient in the old act, is to be welcomed. Benefits can be collected to a maximum of 15 weeks. However, this period was broken down to a maximum of eight weeks previous to confinement, then one week of confinement, and six weeks after confinement.
Babies have a habit of arriving early, due to the uncertainty of the mother as to her exact dates. Complications may arise leading to an early delivery, and in many cases late delivery. By and large, women prefer to work closer to their date of confinement and really, in many cases, they need extra weeks after the confinement rather than before

the confinement. Certainly in a fair percentage of maternity cases the mother may have had unusual complications, or her infant may have developed problems that make it important that she has more time out of the work force after her confinement, both to provide for her own health and that of her child. Certainly this provision is welcomed, and it should certainly have been included in the first place. I think it is fair to say that it was the rigidity of bureaucratic thinking that prevented it from being put in previously.
This bill also removes the built-in work disincentive in that the woman who worked closer to her date of confinement was penalized in favour of those who took leave early. Therefore in the whole concept it has become fairer and, as such, will be welcomed.
Finally, turning to eligibility for regular benefits, several problems arise. Recipients of maternity benefits become eligible for regular benefits when the child is seven weeks old. In certain areas the recipient becomes eligible only when she is actively looking for work and can produce a certificate that child care arrangements have been made.
A survey in the Ottawa-Carleton region by phone turned up the following. There are very few day care centres, and of those surveyed only three made provision for a seven week old child. They all thoroughly discouraged the admission of the seven week old child. Of the estimated 1,000 children under three months, only five are receiving day care. Furthermore, most child day care centres contacted have an average waiting period of four months. In other words, this stipulation under the provision for maternity benefits would essentially disqualify the average mother from receiving any benefits after the initial six week period. I believe this is one area where further government input should be made. Certainly if the woman is a single family parent she may have great difficulty.
So, in summary, Mr. Speaker, this bill does offer improvement over the status quo, but there are indeed some snags which ought to be removed from these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act as proposed in Bill C-16.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Hon. members in all parts of the House are making what, in my view, are excellent speeches in this debate. For the most part they are agreeing that the bill is a necessary one and that it makes progress in the direction of establishing equality between men and women. But member after member is listing the areas and respects in which that equality will not yet be achieved even after the passage of Bill C-16.
I might add that Bill C-52, which will come before us some time later, might also be included among the bills that seek the establish equality. Bill C-52 is one that deals with pension rights under a number of pieces of legislation, and in all of those pieces of legislation it attempts to establish equality between men and women.
It is in this pension area that there is one shortcoming that I should like to mention. There have been discussions, and I believe that there is agreement that the second reading debate on this bill will conclude tonight. Therefore those of us who are now taking part are speaking for even a shorter period of time than was agreed to publicly a short time ago. This is my reason for dealing with just one subject.
I believe that it is a piece of gross unfairness that most pension plans-this is true of the Public Service Superannuation Act, it is true of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, and it is true of the pension plans of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway and many other employers-provide that if there is a survivor pension it works in a strange way. If a man and wife have lived and worked together, presumably they are both responsible for whatever equity they have established. But when retirement time comes, assuming they are both still alive, a pension, whatever its full amount may be, is drawn by the husband. I am speaking of things as they are in most cases.
Now, if the husband dies before the wife, the usual plan is that the widow draws a pension which is only a portion of what her husband's pension was; in most cases it is 50 per cent. In the case of members of parliament, our widows will be entitled to a pension of 60 per cent. But in any case that is the situation. If the husband dies first the widow's pension is only a portion, in most cases 50 per cent. But if the wife dies first and the widower stays on, his pension is not 50 per cent, or 60 per cent, or 75 per cent, it is the whole amount, 100 per cent. We have had this kind of arrangement with us for so long that, like lots of other things, we have accepted it as though it were perfectly proper. I do not think it is.
It seems to me it should not matter which of the marriage partners dies first so far as the amount of the pension that goes to the survivor is concerned. My preference would be that it would be 100 per cent in either case, but if for actuarial reasons in order to get this sort of thing started we have to start with 75 per cent or 90 per cent in either case, let us do so. If it is proper for one of the marriage partners who survives to have a full pension, why does that not apply to the other?
I hope we will soon start to make progress in this field. There is no better place to begin this sort of change in respect of pensions than with those plans which are under
Status of Women
the aegis of the federal government. The Public Service Superannuation Act is a case in point, and our own members of parliament pension plan is another. There are also the plans of the RCMP, the Canadian Armed Forces, and all the other plans that come directly under the government, as well as plans like those of the Canadian National Railways, Air Canada and so on.
As other members have been pointing out today, there is no use boasting about legislation establishing equality when so many areas of inequality remain. I am glad there are some points of equality which have been established under the Canada Pension Plan, and I am glad that under Bill C-52 there a number of instances in which a working woman who dies will be able to leave to her surviving widower the same benefit the working man would leave if he died first and left a surviving widow.
That does not touch this one point I am trying to focus on tonight, namely, that when both partners to the marriage survive into the retirement period, and one dies, why should not the benefits to the survivor be the same whether that survivor is a widow or a widower? I press that point as one that should be considered by the federal government because of the many pension plans for which it is responsible, and I also press the point that those who are dealing with pension plans in private industry should consider this as well.
There is no use muttering about things always having been this way, or about it being the man who has been the one to go out and earn the pension. They have both earned it, and if there is something joint or equal as between men and women let us make it equal all the way. I hope, therefore, that this point is one of those still unfinished bits of business that we will deal with at the earliest possible time. If we believe in equality, let us practice it all the way.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
The other day I received a letter from one of my constituents who wrote:
This letter is to ask you, as my member of parliament, to end the discrimination against women in Canada.
That is quite an opening sentence in the morning mail, and I was already on the defensive because there are limits to our effectiveness. This letter went on to state instances in which the courts have been discriminatory. The writer ended with what baseball writers would describe as a sliding curve by stating:
Please do not answer my letter personally. Use your time and your energy to right the wrong against women in Canada.
I thought that was what this bill and this debate were all about, but where do we start? I read Ms Magazine. I like to think I have been liberated from the chauvinistic thinking of a dying culture in which women's interests were cradle, kitchen, and church. I defend women's right to equal opportunity and equal pay. I have encouraged many women to run for political office since the city councils, legislatures, and parliament of Canada are largely bereft of women's voices. It is ridiculous to have only nine women among the 264 members of parliament. If India, Israel and Ceylon can have women prime ministers, why can we not have more Canadian women in public life? When I look at the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-well, let us not get into that.
If we had more women in public life we would get faster action on those discriminatory blotches that still mar our social landscape; labour and pension inequalities, inequitable executive opportunities, inadequate child care services, and unjust property settlements that degrade husbands and wives. On the other hand, the continuing economic and social handicap that women must surmount in order to succeed in modern society effectively bars many of them from public life.
The politician in me is anxious to proclaim that women's rights must be fully achieved, and that we will not have a truly civilized state until the full status of women is assured. Therefore I give my backing to the Advisory Council on the Status of Women set up by the federal government to give advice on how to implement the 167 recommendations made by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1970.
I give my backing to the present bill, C-16. We cannot afford to continue to waste the talent and potential accomplishments of 50 per cent of the population. These are all sincere statements. They are also politically popular and they might re-assure, somewhat, the women who voted for me. Truthful as they are, these statements are incomplete and they appear to me to be superficial. Politicians can get by with superficial statements. It would be easier not to pursue this subject beyond the black and white answers that can be so easily projected to the electorate. The full truth is that I am profoundly disturbed by the relationship of the women's rights movement to the over-all question of full humanism in modern life.

What I am concerned about is value conflict. Professor Charles Hobart, a sociologist at the University of Alberta, expresses the conflict well:
The family depends upon and symbolizes inefficient values of being, knowing, caring, loving, unconditionally committing oneself. These values are incompatible with the urban industrial values of production, achievement, exchange, quantification, efficiency, success. Simultaneous unlimited commitment to people and love and concern-and to achievement, success and prosperity-is impossible.
It is disruptive and potentially incapacitating to try to accommodate both sets of values. Because men all too often sacrifice success in marriage for success in careers, should women too choose the dehumanizing urban values as the criterion for success? What business is this of the politician? Why does he not stick to the clear issue of removing discrimination against women?
Again I say that it is not enough to take a single-minded view. I want to say with respect to the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo), who made what I have already described as a courageous and fighting speech tonight, that I would encourage her as she considers the role of women in modern society, to which she addressed herself tonight, by saying that she will enhance and strengthen her case by taking a much larger view than that of abortion.
Most of the hon. member's speech concerned abortion. I would encourage her, having the feeling she has which I respect, to persuade her colleagues in the government to have a full and major debate on abortion. However, I say to her with respect that when she delivers a speech on women's rights, three quarters or four fifths of which were devoted to the subject of abortion, she does her cause a very serious injustice.
I cannot separate women from the totality of society any more that I can separate men. To express genuine concern about the attack on marriage as an institution and families as the central cell of our society, is not to diminish the need for women's rights. The two subjects must be fitted together. If that is not seen to be the job of the lonely politician, it is certainly the responsibility of the government in creating an economic and social climate that enhances the fulfillment of family life. I thought that was what International Women's Year would involve, and that parliament would be responding to that. I have not heard anything like that tonight.
I think that the status of the family may well become one of the explosive political issues in the decades ahead. The considerable talk today about complusory contraception, abortion, and sterilization indicates a foundation for state intervention in the name of quality of life. There is now abundant literature arguing against marriage in the traditional sense, and the increasing divorce rates reveal the de facto instability of the marriage institution. I will not take up the time of the House tonight to go through the divorce statistics.
Much of the new wave of thinking is suffused with the belief that the family is a tyrannical and decadent institution that needs to be replaced. In this view women should be liberated from child-rearing, mothers being an outdated occupational group. The door is then opened to those who would bypass reactionary parents by control systems that
May 29, 1975

would not only biologically engineer children but program their social and cultural environment. The point I want to make now is that what is needed especially is an application of law that accords women their human rights and, at the same time, strengthens family, and hence human, life. This principle is valid whether a woman marries or not; there simply cannot be an artificial line drawn between the feminist movement and the general society, of which the family is the core.
In fact, we increase the serious political and psychological risks by continuing to frustrate such a sense of connection between the individual and society. Whether we focus on politics or family development, our aim should be to lessen the antagonism between the sexes and also between government and its women citizens. The point of women's liberation, as I see it, is not to create a new dominance but rather to make possible the fullest participation of women in the human conversation. In short, both men and women are responsible for changes in relationships that will have deep consequences for our children, and we may not escape such responsibility by focussing only on our own emancipation. Increased freedom should increase, not decrease, accountability.
What this argument boils down to, in practical terms, is the ability of people to experience other people as real, as human. That depends to a large extent on the ability of children to experience deep and lasting relationships with adults. Some institution must exist in our society to do this. Call it a family. Give it permanence. Help youth to grasp the idea that human beings are not manipulatory conveniences, floating in and out of the realms of life, to be disposed of with the rest of the junk in our throw-away society.
The resistance of people to the throw-away mentality depends on the depth of their experiences with other people-the kind of experiences that are developed in a family. It is essential for young children in particular to have secure relationships. This is primary not only to the well being of the child but to the stability of future society composed of individuals who are reasonably secure, reasonably strong. The way in which these relationships have been provided to children historically is by women. Today women want to do other things, one of the manifestations of women's liberation. They may be able to, but they cannot discard overnight their historic contribution to the development of children in the name of occupational rights.
Day care centres have value but they are not the total solution, nor should women shrug off their responsibilities by pointing to day care centres. I am saying that until I can be confident that the full human support the family gives a child can be protected I am cautious about women's liberation.
Reverting to my responsibility as a member of parliament, I look for social policies that will help families to stay together and develop the potential of all within the family. This certainly extends beyond voting for increased family allowances, which is the easy way out for the government in meeting its responsibilities. Every policy, whether it be economic, cultural, social, recreational, affects families in some way of course. We must begin to see more clearly the impact that they all have on human
Status of Women
relationships. As William Dyson, executive director of the Vanier Institute of the Family says:
We must go deeply into what we mean by law, which now reflects the machine world so heavily, and recognize fully that if we want a family policy that is truly applicable and useful, we have no choice but to perceive the whole of public policy as critical to our future as persons, as families, in our groups and in our society.
We are back again to the need to change our priorities in policy making so that people, not economic growth, come first. As a member of parliament, then, I am concerned with monitoring the consequences of policies and programs which may seem unrelated but actually make up the total social community. I have to learn to live with the fact that I do not have all the answers. Even being able to ask the right questions about the direction of society is a sizeable accomplishment these days.
I ask these questions in the framework of a set of values, that the good of everybody, women, men and children, be taken into account. One of the ways in which this total approach works out is seen in wages. A man today cannot afford to give up his job and have the family exist on his wife's earnings because women ordinarily earn less than men. But if her earning power were as great as a man's then the wife could, when desired, be the sole bread-winner, allowing her husband to manage the home or explore new interests. Thus women's rights could work for the liberation of men.
This larger view of women's rights was expressed by Sylvia Gelber, director of the Women's Bureau of the federal Department of Labour, who favours a bills of rights entrenched in the constitution of Canada to provide for women's equity before the law, as follows:
If carefully drafted, it might also provide for other groups of people, people who are young; people who are old; people who are disabled; people who are poor; as well as people who are female, be they single or married, that even-handed justice which is the goal of those concerned with the well-being of our people and of our country.
In this way we can see women's rights as part of the whole human rights field that has occupied international attention since the end of World War II. When the universal declaration of human rights was adopted in 1948, fundamental rights were declared to be the right of all without distinction, including sex.
The United Nations has, in the meantime, devoted more energy to ridding the world of racial discrimination than sexual. Some specialized agencies have, however, adopted a number of conventions affecting the rights of women in such fields as education and employment. The International Labour Organization has adopted a number of conventions affecting the rights of women in all conditions of employment, including recruitment, promotions and pay. The I.L.O. conventions have been ratified by Canada, leading to the passage of anti-discriminatory legislation here-although it took the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women to produce clear legislation outlawing sexual discrimination.
Even now, however, more legislation is needed to amend the Canada Labour Code to ensure equal access to job opportunities; amendments to the federal Superannuation Act are needed to ensure equal pension and fringe benefit rights; there should be equality for women and inclusion

May 29, 1975
Status of Women
of homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan; and there should be proportionate appointment to and employment by federal boards, commissions and Crown corporations.
The Canadian Bill of Rights, passed in 1960, was designed to provide, within the area of federal jurisdiction, equality before the law without distinction on grounds of sex. But, as Miss Gelber notes;
The courts have generally interpreted the Bill of Rights in such a way as to assume that parliament did not intend by its provisions to alter other federal laws which might have been interpreted as being inconsistent with the Bill of Rights.
Because of the limitations of this federal statute, a stronger instrument is needed to override any existing statute that allows discrimination. The laws in a number of provinces contain a variety of discriminatory clauses affecting women, particularly in the fields of family law, welfare and property rights. Welfare legislation often operates to the disadvantage of women, frequently denying equity on grounds of personal morality. We have not touched on that contentious issue tonight.
The assurance of equal rights in the provincial field is required as well as in the federal. This is what has led to the clear need for Ottawa and the provinces to agree on a constitutional bill of rights-even though this goal is a very elusive one. The establishment of the federal Human Rights Commission to enforce anti-discrimination laws is a step toward this goal because it will help to strengthen public attitudes concerning justice.

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STATUTE LAW (STATUS OF WOMEN) AMENDMENT ACT, 1974 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH EQUALITY OF STATUS FOR MALE AND FEMALE PERSONS UNDER CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before proceeding I would like to refer to what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) noted, namely, that there were not too many women present to speak in the House on the subject before us. May I point out that most women would prefer to hear men speak on the subject of inequality with regard to women.
Also, I would like to point out the active role that women politicians, at least from our side, are presently playing. Madam Speaker was in the chair during the debate; the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) has spoken, as we know; the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin) is in Europe with the parliamentary committee; the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is at the meeting of the Standing Committee on Immigration Policy; the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) was to speak this afternoon but had to be called away; and the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) has been in the House all evening during debate of this important topic and has spoken on it on many other occasions.
It is indeed with pleasure that I rise to close the debate on this bill called by many the omnibus bill but really called the Statute Law (Status of Women) Amendment Act 1974, and to see it go to committee, following which, I hope, it will come back here soon on the road to its final destination.
The bill, can only help all Canadians. As we know, it amends certain acts to provide equality under these statutes for male and female persons. The government, following the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, and of many organizations and individuals, has sought to do away with the provisions in eight pieces of legislation which discriminate against women or are otherwise prejudicial to women.
Among others, this bill will deal with the Canada Elections Act which will have one set of rules for listing electors. Information will now be descriptive of the elector in terms of the name, address, occupation and sex of the elector.
The Criminal Code will have two changes. No longer will there be presumption of coercion of the woman by her
May 29, 1975

spouse under section 23(3). In addition, section 197 will be amended to make it obligatory for married women to provide the necessities of life for their spouses. This puts the same onus on both spouses.
The National Defence Act will allow girls to be treated the same as boys-all as cadets. The Unemployment Insurance Act will also be amended to make a flexible 15 week period for maternity benefits, something which I am sure most pregnant women merited in the past and will have in the future. Other acts to be amended are the Immigration Act, the Public Service Employment Act, the Pension Act, and the Civil War Pensions and Allowances Act.
The government has also moved amendment to the Canada Pension Plan, one of the most significant being provision of full equality for male and female contributors and beneficiaries under the act.
Presently before the House there is the citizenship bill which, among other things, will grant citizenship for either the male or the female parent. It is also anticipated that the Human Rights Commission legislation will be brought to the House, as well as amendments to the Criminal Code in respect of rape and other sexual offences. All these amendments can only show the ability of this government to recognize the need for providing equal treatment for men and women.
However, attitudes will not change in Canada simply by enforcing legislation. One must remember that we are striving for equality between men and women on the basis of freedom of choice of work, freedom of choice of environment, and freedom to choose something other than existing ideas which categorized women in the past as being designated to one role.
Young people today are moving that way in a much easier fashion. There will be no stumbling blocks. They know what they want. I will quote from the magazine Ms., a letter from Anita Buzick II of Killeen, Texas:
When I saw that in my spelling book they had "The Queen is the wife of a King", I got really mad. Even though I'm only nine years old, and only in the fourth grade, I've written five poems. One from the five I thought you might want to put in Ms.
Here it is:
If you think I'm going to slave in the kitchen for a man who is supposed to be brave,
Then I'm sorry to say, but you're wrong all the way,
Because I'm going to be an astronaut.
These ideas are among our young coming up. No longer will young boys and girls be thought of in different directions. They are going to go after the same jobs whether they be in construction, teaching, medicine or any of the other fields.
I, being a parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), at any time in the short while in this position have had to clarify that I am a member of parliament and that being a parliamentary secretary is only for a member of parliament. It is always assumed when I appear to represent the minister
Status of Women
that I must be one of the secretaries from withjn the department. This, I am sure, does not happen with the opposite sex because secretaries have always been designated female.
It is my understanding that a statement was made this afternoon in the House to the effect that every woman should have the choice to stay at home and be a housewife if she chooses. I agree with this commendable statement, but I would like to point out that it is the type of statement which creates an attitude, and a false one. One should say, rather, every person, instead of delegating the role of the home to a woman. While on the same statement I would like to go one step further and define choice.
In the past women had the choice to go out and work for a few years at some defined position which belonged to being a woman, and then to get married and have a family. There was no choice in this accepted role. The woman had to find a husband because she could not survive, for the most part, on the amount she could bring in and, under the circumstances, which would eventually offer no challenge to her. She therefore accepted to be challenged as a housewife without being able to choose any other role to fulfill herself. Equality in our society in the future will allow all people to choose a role and to further themselves within that role to the extent that their choices were educated and not designated by society to be fulfilled.
Under circumstances where women are employed and earning the same amount as men, perhaps at that point one can have an educated choice either to pursue the role within the working world or to stay at home, raise a family and be the supportive element to the working spouse. But for this person it will have been chosen and will become a career. This type of choice can only enhance family life.
At present there is probably under utilization of half the talent in this country. This can only show that both men and women are losers and that the country as a whole becomes a loser. Role stereotyping is damaging to men as well as to women, and true equality can only be good for both sexes.
I would like to speak for a few minutes on the economic discrepancies which exist and which it is hoped will be changed before too long by legislation at the federal level, such as the Human Rights Commission, and surely all provinces will bring this type of legislation into play in respect to provincial government jobs. However, to further heighten this point I would like to read from "Women's Bureau '74" put out by Labour Canada, at page 39:
The average employment earnings of full-time full-year male babysitters were more than twice (127.5 per cent) those of female babysitters during 1970. In a world where we have become accustomed to looking on certain kinds of occupations as male and female, this interesting fact appears to be somewhat ironic. Yet it is not the only occupation generally viewed as female in which male workers show average employment earnings in excess of those of the female workers in the same occupation.
Among the professions, for example, that of librarian is generally viewed as a female profession; yet the average employment earnings of men librarians exceed those of women by almost one-fifth (18.6 per cent). Similarly, the professions of dietitians and nutritionists are generally looked upon as female; yet male workers in these professions derive average employment earnings almost one-quarter (22.6 per cent) more than the female workers. Another example of an occupation that at one time was looked upon as male, but, in recent years, has

May 29, 1975
Status of Women
tended to become female is that of tellers and cashiers; yet the average employment earnings of male workers in these occupations are one-half (50.9 per cent) greater than those of female workers.
Madam Speaker, I now turn to page 43 to read a little bit further about this economic discrepancy as follows:
In so far as the gap in earnings between men and women in the labour force is concerned, disparities are all too evident. In fact, in terms of actual dollars earned, there is evidence that in many instances the gap is a widening one. For example, between the years 1969 and 1972, the dollar gap between the reported earnings of men and women workers widened in 37 out of 74 occupations.
The broadening of the dollar gap, it would appear, is due primarily to the widespread practice of increasing wage rates on a flat percentage basis. Thus, for example, if in a given occupation, a male worker is paid $3.00 an hour and a female worker is paid $2.50 an hour, the effect of a flat rate 6 per cent increase is to widen the dollar gap between the two.
The remedy lies not only in achieving at long last the principle of equal pay for equal work but in opening up opportunities in the work world for women workers so as to remove existing obstacles to full participation in the Canadian economy. One of the means of achieving this end is by ensuring that women prepare themselves academically and technically through the existing institutions of higher learning as well as the technical schools of the country.
It is very easy for the members of the opposition as well as organizations to say that the government has not done enough. However, it is only recently that an awareness among 51 per cent of the population has started to take effect. It is only through those situations arising from their jobs that women can now begin to concentrate on what is dissatisfying, concentrating and organizing to use their very powerful 51 per cent to register their dissatisfaction and ask for more education, more legislation, to obtain more jobs of importance. This way women will be giving their own input to affect other women, such as the demand that all provinces obtain day care centres.
For example, in the case of women lawyers when a client comes to an office on a family matter most often the male lawyer cannot help but look at her and say "I suppose if I were married to her I would divorce her too, or separate from her" and the female lawyer deals with the matter. This is common amongst most male lawyers-at least the ones who have brought it to my attention.
Women are beginning to waken up to the fact that they too can do the job. Awareness of this fact will change attitudes, and time will bring this about. It is easy to hide behind the "do something" syndrome when women themselves do not know what to do because of the mixed feelings they have about their own role. It is not just by providing legislation that we will change and become equal-it is by attempting to change attitudes and make people aware that women can do the job equally as well as men, be it in the working world, be it at technical schools, be it at universities, be it in government, or be it in the homes.

subtopic: FINANCE-SUGGESTED REVIEW OF REDUCTION OF TARIFF ON TIRES
FINANCE-SUGGESTED REVIEW OF REDUCTION OF TARIFF ON TIRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the other day I directed a number of questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) concerning difficulties being experienced in the Canadian auto tire production industry. The answers I received were quite unsatisfactory. Therefore I wish to pursue the matter further at this time in the adjournment debate.
We have witnessed recently yet another example of Liberal government economic policy putting Canadians on unstable economic ground. At Whitby Tire at Whitby, Ontario, 290 workers were indefinitely laid off. The company cites the economic slow-down in the auto industry as the cause, but the facts dispute this. Sales figures show that the volume of sales has increased slightly, although the profits are down somewhat. Obviously from the company's point of view, the decision was a micro-economic decision based solely on the profit maximization principle.
The United Rubber Workers, who incidentally report 2,000 of their 18,000 workers laid off, see part of the reason for the Whitby lay-off as the result of a tariff reduction from 17 Vi per cent to 12 Vi per cent on imported tires and tubes. This, without doubt, is a contributing factor, but the scope goes well beyond the tariff rate.
Since 1965 Canada has had a trading deficit in the rubber tire and tube industry every year with the exception of 1967. The total deficit to the end of 1974 was $298 million. The deficit for 1974 alone was $155 million, an increase of 600 per cent from 1973, and the trend shows no sign of change. The trade figures for January and February, 1975, show a $24 million deficit, itself equal to the whole deficit of 1973.
The causes for this jump are quite clear. In 1974 the companies tried to break a strike in the Canadian industry by importing American tires. The American parent of Whitby Tire, Firestone, increased their product imports at that time in an unsuccessful bid to circumvent the strike. Now that the American parent has a strong established foothold in the Canadian market, what use is there for a small subsidiary such as Whitby?
How many Canadian jobs must be lost before the government and its supporters realize that Canada must take positive steps to control its own economy? How many jobs of Canadian workers will be sacrificed to benefit United States parent companies before the government realizes that the Foreign Investment Review Act must be revised and tightly enforced? When is the government going to institute quotas as a stipulation in its tire-import-export trade?
The problem, as illustrated by Whitby Tire, is that Canadian plants do not have a reasonable share of the
May 29, 1975

North American market. The Liberal government is guilty of mismanagement and indifference. The workers of Whitby Tire, especially the 290 laid off, would be the last to agree that the Firestone takeover of Whitby Tire is of "significant benefit to Canada", as required by the Foreign Investment Review Act concerning Firestone's takeover of the company.
Is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) prepared to review, along with his colleague, the Minister of Finance, the decision to reduce the tariff rate from 17Yi per cent to 12V4 per cent? Is the minister prepared to consult with the tire industry officials to work out a means of recapturing Canada's rightful market share? These questions have been asked before but responses have not been forthcoming. The question boils down to whether or not the government really cares about the thousands of rubber workers and their future.
The Department of Finance took some interest, for it invited the presidents of the Canadian tire industry to Ottawa so as to ascertain their plans for expansion and employment. Was a bleak picture presented? Quite possibly, because the department did not inform the union or this House as to what transpired. The only statement forthcoming was that at the present time there was no need to increase the tariff to its previous level of 17 % per cent. The fact remains that the present reduced tariff acts only as an incentive to import tires and as a disincentive to the Canadian industry and the workers directly and indirectly dependent on it.
Some will argue that an increased tariff would increase the price of tires. However, the reduction in the tariff has not reduced tire prices. I see no reason why an increased tariff should increase prices. The fact remains that United States and Canadian tire prices are similar, and claims that imported U.S. tires are cheaper are simply unfounded.
We in the New Democratic Party feel the government must protect Canadian industry and Canadian jobs. I ask that the minister take action to restore Canada's share of the tire market. Our working people have rights, and must not be left to the mercy of U.S. based multinationals. The Canadian tire industry must not be allowed to die.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-SUGGESTED REVIEW OF REDUCTION OF TARIFF ON TIRES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me say at the outset that the government shares the hon. member's concern about the current employment situation in the rubber industry. The question is whether this is due to the increase in imports as such and, more particularly, to any increase which may have been occasioned by the reduction in the tariff, or whether it is a result of the general situation in the automotive industry.
Hon. members will be aware that this tariff reduction was one of a number of tariff cuts originally introduced in the budget of February, 1973, as part of the government's program for moderating inflation. The legislation gave the governor in council authority to restore the original rates of duty if circumstances warranted such action.
Following the introduction of the November budget the United Rubber Workers' Union requested the government to restore the 17 Vi per cent rate. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) directed his officials to carry out a full investigation of the situation and to report back to him.
Adjournment Debate
Officials of the Department of Finance and of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce met frequently with representatives of the United Rubber Workers. Officials of the two departments also sought the views of the major tire companies. The companies attributed the increase in imports to the decision of the automobile manufacturers to equip their new models with radials sooner than had been expected. This had taken place before planned expansion of radial tire production in Canada had come on stream. I am given to understand that some of these new plants will be in production shortly.
The union and the companies were asked to submit additional information concerning the outlook for employment and production in the industry. I understand that on the basis of this data a more detailed report has now been made to the Minister of Finance. It will, of course, be up to the minister to decide what further action may be necessary once he has studied the report. So, contrary to what the hon. member has said, there has been consultation, not only with the tire companies but with the union.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GARRISON DIVERSION-SUGGESTION UNITED STATES BE ASKED FOR A MORATORIUM ON PROJECT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GARRISON DIVERSION-SUGGESTION UNITED STATES BE ASKED FOR A MORATORIUM ON PROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the second time within nine days that I have risen to ask the government to call for a moratorium to halt the Garrison diversion project in North Dakota. On May 20 I gave reasons why a moratorium should be sought. One of them was a statement made by Mr. Charles A. Vanik, the Ohio representative, that the Garrison project was "environmental and economic madness." Mr. Vanik added:
The Bureau of Reclamation has tried to do everything in its power to push the Garrison project ahead. Nothing can hide the fact, however, that it is an environmental disaster.
I presented new evidence to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) today and I propose to read a letter in just a moment or two. On May 20 the parliamentary secretary stated that the Canadian government would be sending a blunt note, along with the United States government, to the International Joint Commission, calling for another study. The last thing we want is another study into the Garrison diversion project. If time allowed, I could stand here for three hours quoting from studies showing why this project should not be proceeded with. It is unfortunate that the government is not looking at these studies because it would then know that it should be calling for a moratorium, not a further study.
What is also most disappointing is that the Schreyer government of Manitoba has gone along with this proposal that a note be sent to the IJC for another study. I note that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is here tonight, and I hope that he will use his influence to contact Premier Schreyer and ask him to get together with the federal government in calling for a moratorium.
Today I forwarded a letter to the Acting Prime Minister from William S. Moorhead, who is the chairman of the

May 29, 1975
Adjournment Debate
conservation, energy and natural resources sub-committee in the United States, to the Hon. Henry A. Kissinger, Secretary of State, dated March 19, 1975. The letter reads as follows:
Recently, the General Accounting Office and your department have concluded that "as presently proposed", the Garrison Diversion United in North Dakota, which the Interior Department is now constructing, "would likely result" in pollution of Canadian waters "in violation of Article IV of the Boundary Waters Treaty with Canada". Interior does not dispute this conclusion.
Despite this, Interior is continuing to construct the project as now planned. Indeed, in a February 28, 1975 letter to our subcommittee, Interior states that "adoption of significantly revised alternative plan of development" to avoid a treaty violation "would require new or amended legislative authority."
It has been suggested at recent joint U.S.-Canadian meetings that the matter be referred to the International Joint Commission (IJC). But in the meantime, the Interior Department is continuing to build the project which is now 18 per cent completed.
I do not object to such a referral. But I find it difficult to understand how the United States can justify continued construction of a project which is certain to result in a Treaty violation.
I hope the parliamentary secretary has some firm answer on this subject tonight, and will not simply say that we are just going to send off another little note to the IJC.
Assurances that the project will not be allowed to result in a treaty violation are empty since there is no indication any alternatives proposed by Interior will ever be acceptable to Canada or Congress. As more money is expended and more of the project completed, it will become increasingly difficult from a political point of view in the United States to halt the project if the IJC finds that no viable alternatives exist-
Mr. Moorhead went on to say:
I strongly share that doubt. I think it is time the United States face up to the fact that our treaty obligations with Canada require a moratorium on further contracting for this project until a viable alternative is developed. Such a moratorium should not result in any costs to the United States. I urge that you take the lead in establishing such a moratorium.
That is very strong language, Madam Speaker, and we cannot ignore it. In another letter from the United States Department of the Interior Commissioner of Reclamation to the deputy under secretary, it is stated, among other things, that the United States will have to do studies into field data for potential pumping plant sites, damsites, canal alignments, desalting plants and brine disposal sites, some in Manitoba, with considerable assistance from outside agencies. The letter goes on:
The March 11, 1975, memorandum from the Assistant Secretary- Land and Water Resources to you recommended that the studies be "informal" and not made available to "local interests nor to the Canadians."
So they are suppressing information from us. This is reason enough to call for this moratorium, and not just send some silly note off to the IJC.
It further states:
Further study of the alternatives at a level below feasibility grade, but sufficient to provide a closer look at the viability of the alternatives in sufficient time to properly consider the request for funding on the construction of the Velva Canal, can be completed by June 1976
In a press release issued yesterday by the Prairie Environmental Defence League Inc. it is stated:
U.S. Officials Conspire to keep Canadians in dark over Garrison project.

Desalinization plants and brine disposal fields are in store for Manitobans because of the Garrison Diversion project in North Dakota, according to George Heshka, chairman of the Prairie Environmental Defence League. The desalinization plants and brine disposal fields, a U.S. compromise to pollution of the Souris River, were named as alternatives by Gilbert Stamms, commissioner of the Bureau of Reclamation, in a memo to the deputy under secretary of the department of the interior (attached). In the memo, Stamms said some of the brine disposal fields would be located in Manitoba.
Heshka charged the bureau with "deceit and secrecy" in not reporting the possibility of brine disposal fields to Manitobans and Canadians. Stamms said, "he concurred that studies (concerning desalinization plants and brine disposal fields) should be informal and not made available to local interests nor to the Canadians-"

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member keeps insisting on what he calls a moratorium. To start with, I will just quote what I said on May 20, as recorded at page 5955 of Hansard:
In February, 1974, the United States government gave assurances that the United States would honour its obligations under the treaty-
I was referring to the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty. I went on to state:
-the United States would honour its obligation under the treaty and pledged that no project construction potentially affecting waters flowing into Canada would be undertaken unless it were clear that these United States obligations under the treaty would be met.
We have no reason to believe that the United States will not honour its commitment after giving us assurances that it would.
In view of our concern over the potential adverse effects of the Garrison project, as currently envisaged, we are of course pleased to learn, if the press reports are accurate as to the contents of this document, that the Bureau of Reclamation is examining alternatives to the current project. However, I would note that our ongoing discussions with the United States are being conducted at gov-ernment-to-government level, and not at the level of the Bureau of Reclamation. I am confident that no significant information relevant to the Garrison project as it affects Canada will be withheld by either side, in keeping with the traditional candour and frankness which characterizes our exchanges with the United States.
The United States has assured us that no decision on construction involving any diversion of water into the Souris Basin would be undertaken prior to 1978. United States officials have further stated that, under the present timetable, construction of the Velva Canal is not scheduled to begin until 1980, and construction on the Souris River is not to begin until 1981. In this regard we are confident that the United States will honour its long standing pledge that no project construction potentially affecting waters flowing into Canada would be undertaken unless it were clear that the United States could meet its obligation under Article IV of the Boundary Waters Treaty not to pollute water crossing the boundary "to the injury of health or property" in Canada. We are, of course, in continuing consultation with the United States government on the question of project schedules as they might affect Canada. We shall, however, seek official re-affirma-
May 29, 1975

tion from the U.S. government that our understanding of the construction schedules is correct.

May 29, 1975

On account of continued increase of cost of living it has been decided to escalate CN pensions effective January 1, 1975 on the following basis:
Retirement in Pensioners monthly Widows monthly flat rate increase flat rate increase
1967 or prior

This approach gives pensioners and widows who retired before the benefits became payable under the Canada/Que-bec Pension Plan, the largest increase (6%) tapering each
year as benefits under these plans increased. No increase is being granted to pensioners who retired in 1973 and 1974, since they have benefited substantially from the improvements in the CN pension plan effective January 1, 1973.
The cost of escalating on this basis has been estimated by our acturaries at $2,230,400.00 per annum over an amortization of 17 years, 9 months in accordance with the pension benefits standards act.
Advice of the new increases will be sent to recipient with their June pension cheques and the increase including arrears to January 1, 1975 will be reflected in their pension cheques as soon as possible thereafter.
At the end of 1973 we had increased contributory pension on account of the cost of living by 2% for all years back to 1935. The latest increase applicable to all pensioners in payment on December 31, 1973 was 4% effective January 1, 1974.
